name: Israel
governanceModel: Sectoral, risk-based guidance without a binding AI-specific law
debateTopics: AI21 Labs' decline and what it signals about the Israeli AI startup boom
Israel's principle-based approach without a binding AI law as models scale
Military and defence AI use and international-law scrutiny
overview:
Israel has no single AI Act. The Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology (MIST) leads sectoral AI policy through its December 2023 'Responsible Innovation' policy — a risk-based approach built on human oversight, transparency and accountability, developed jointly with the Ministry of Justice. In May 2026, MIST, the Ministry of Justice and the Israel National Digital Agency published version 1.0 of a 'Guide for Responsible AI Use in the Public Sector.' On June 16, 2026 the government also approved a new National AI Program for 2027–2032, led by a newly created National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office and reportedly targeting around 100,000 processing units and $20–30B in compute investment — a notable expansion of the state's role alongside MIST's existing framework.

Israel's private AI and tech sector presents a mixed picture. Google (Alphabet) completed a $32B cash acquisition of the Israeli cybersecurity company Wiz in March 2026 — reportedly the largest acquisition in Google's history and among the highest-profile exits for an Israeli tech company — while AI21 Labs, once a $1.4B unicorn, has shrunk sharply, laying off around 110 of its 180 staff and scaling back most standalone product lines in favour of its Maestro agent-orchestration platform.

currentDirection.summary: Israel continues layering non-binding, sectoral AI guidance through MIST with a newly approved national compute strategy: in June 2026 the government approved a National AI Program for 2027–2032, led by a new National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office and reportedly targeting roughly 100,000 processing units and $20–30B in compute investment. How this expanded, infrastructure-focused strategy will interact with MIST's existing 'Responsible Innovation' framework, and whether Israel eventually moves toward binding AI-specific rules, remains to be seen.

recentDevelopments.text: NVIDIA deepens its Israeli chip-design and AI-infrastructure R&D footprint: it moved into an expanded Be'er Sheva R&D centre (reported to roughly triple its footprint, with hundreds of planned hires) and unveiled plans for a multibillion-shekel campus in the northern town of Kiryat Tivon — part of a reported ~$1.5B expansion — reinforcing Israel's role in advanced networking and data-centre silicon design even without a domestic frontier lab.

researchEcosystem.summary: Israeli AI research runs through Technion, Tel Aviv University, Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Weizmann Institute's dedicated Institute for Artificial Intelligence. According to one industry ranking, Technion and Tel Aviv University place among the world's top ten universities for startup founders produced, with their alumni reportedly having raised roughly $23B and $30B respectively — these figures have not been independently re-verified and should be treated with some caution.

debates.topic: AI21 Labs' decline and what it signals about the Israeli AI startup boom
debates.summary: AI21 Labs' collapse from a $1.4B unicorn to roughly 70 employees stands as a sharp counterpoint to parts of Israel's broader AI-startup success narrative.
debates.expanded: While Wiz's $32B acquisition by Google and strong university-founder metrics point to parts of a thriving ecosystem, AI21 Labs' decline suggests that even well-funded Israeli frontier-model ambitions can struggle against better-resourced US and Chinese labs. Some observers read this as evidence that Israel's comparative strength lies more in applied AI and cybersecurity than in frontier foundation-model competition, though this remains a contested reading given the small number of Israeli frontier-model attempts to draw on.

debates.topic: Israel's principle-based approach without a binding AI law as models scale
debates.summary: As generative AI and agentic systems grow more capable, some observers argue Israel's non-binding Responsible Innovation framework faces the same test other soft-law jurisdictions do.
debates.expanded: MIST's approach has so far relied on sectoral guidance rather than binding rules, on the view that flexibility outweighs enforceability. The government's June 2026 approval of a large-scale National AI Program is focused primarily on compute infrastructure rather than binding legal rules, so it does not by itself resolve this question. Whether Israel eventually moves toward firmer AI-specific rules as frontier capabilities scale remains an open debate among policy observers.

debates.topic: Military and defence AI use and international-law scrutiny
debates.summary: Reporting on the Israel Defense Forces' use of AI decision-support systems in Gaza — notably tools described in investigative coverage as 'Lavender' and 'Where's Daddy?' — has made Israel a focal point in the global debate over AI in targeting and accountability under international humanitarian law.
debates.expanded: Investigative outlets reported that AI systems were used to help generate and track large numbers of potential targets, with critics — including human-rights groups and some defence analysts — arguing that heavy reliance on algorithmic target-generation, combined with limited human review, raised serious civilian-protection and international-law concerns; the IDF has contested key characterisations, describing such tools as decision-support aids subject to human judgement rather than autonomous weapons. The episode is frequently cited as an example of military AI outpacing binding legal and ethical guardrails, and it sits largely outside MIST's civilian 'Responsible Innovation' framework, which does not comprehensively govern defence uses. Specific operational claims remain contested and difficult to verify independently.
